items.new: That night in bed, we worked out our plans for the next day. But to my surprise and no small concern, Queequeg now gave me to understand that he had been diligently consulting Yojo — the name of his little black god — and Yojo had told him two or three times over, and strongly insisted on it in every way, that instead of the two of us going together among the whaling fleet in the harbor and choosing our ship jointly — instead of this, I say, Yojo earnestly directed that the choice of the ship should rest entirely with me, since Yojo meant to befriend us. To that end he had already picked out a vessel which I, Ishmael, left to myself, would be certain to hit upon, exactly as though it had happened by chance. And I was to sign on to that vessel immediately, leaving Queequeg out of it for the present.

items.new: Now, this plan of Queequeg's — or rather Yojo's — about choosing our ship: I didn't like that plan at all. I had counted a good deal on Queequeg's shrewdness to point out the whaler best fitted to carry us and our fortunes safely. But since all my objections had no effect on Queequeg, I had to give in; and so I got ready to go at the business with a determined, rushing sort of energy and vigor that would quickly settle that trifling little affair. Early the next morning, I left Queequeg shut up with Yojo in our little bedroom — for it seemed that for Queequeg and Yojo that day was some sort of Lent or Ramadan, a day of fasting, humiliation, and prayer. How it worked I never could find out, because though I applied myself to it several times, I never could master his liturgies and his Thirty-Nine Articles. Leaving Queequeg, then, fasting over his tomahawk pipe, and Yojo warming himself at his sacrificial fire of wood shavings, I set out among the shipping. After a long stretch of wandering and many random inquiries, I learned that there were three ships taking on crews for three-year voyages — the Devil-dam, the Tit-bit, and the Pequod. Devil-Dam, I don't know the origin of; Tit-bit is obvious; Pequod, you will no doubt remember, was the name of a celebrated tribe of Massachusetts Indians, now as extinct as the ancient Medes. I peered and pried around the Devil-dam; from her I hopped over to the Tit-bit; and finally, going aboard the Pequod and looking around her for a moment, I decided that this was the very ship for us.

items.new: You may have seen many a quaint craft in your day, for all I know — square-toed luggers, mountainous Japanese junks, butter-box galliots, and whatnot. But take my word for it, you never saw such a rare old craft as this same rare old Pequod. She was a ship of the old school, rather small if anything, with an old-fashioned, claw-footed look about her. Long seasoned and weather-stained in the typhoons and calms of all four oceans, her old hull's complexion was darkened like that of a French grenadier who has fought in both Egypt and Siberia. Her venerable bows looked bearded. Her masts — cut somewhere on the coast of Japan, where her original ones were lost overboard in a gale — her masts stood stiffly up like the spines of the three old kings of Cologne. Her ancient decks were worn and wrinkled, like the pilgrim-worshipped flagstone in Canterbury Cathedral where Becket bled. But to all these old antiquities of hers were added new and marvelous features, belonging to the wild business she had followed for more than half a century. Old Captain Peleg, for many years her chief mate before he commanded a vessel of his own, and now a retired seaman and one of the principal owners of the Pequod — this old Peleg, during his time as chief mate, had built upon her original grotesqueness and inlaid it all over with a quaintness of both material and design unmatched by anything, unless it be Thorkill-Hake's carved buckler or bedstead. She was decked out like some barbaric Ethiopian emperor, his neck heavy with pendants of polished ivory. She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, dressing herself up in the carved bones of her enemies. All around, her unpaneled, open bulwarks were garnished like one continuous jaw with the long, sharp teeth of the sperm whale, set there as pins to fasten her old hempen sinews and tendons to. Those sinews did not run through lowly blocks of land wood but traveled deftly over sheaves of sea-ivory. Scorning a turnstile wheel at her reverend helm, she sported a tiller there; and that tiller was in one piece, curiously carved from the long, narrow lower jaw of her hereditary foe. The helmsman who steered by that tiller in a storm felt like the Tartar holding back his fiery steed by clutching its jaw. A noble craft, but somehow a most melancholy one! All noble things are touched with that.

items.new: When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, so as to offer myself as a candidate for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't very well overlook a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, pitched a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be only a temporary structure used in port. It was cone-shaped, some ten feet high, made of the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of the right whale's jaws. A circle of these slabs, planted with their broad ends on the deck and laced together, sloped in toward one another and joined at the top in a tufted point, where the loose, hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on some old Pottowottamie Sachem's (chief's) head. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, so that whoever sat inside had a complete view forward.

items.new: Sitting on the stern bench was what struck me as a most unusual and surprising figure. This turned out to be Captain Bildad, who along with Captain Peleg was one of the largest owners of the vessel. The remaining shares, as is sometimes the case in these ports, were held by a crowd of old pensioners — widows, orphaned children, and wards of the court — each owning about the value of a timber head, a foot of plank, or a nail or two in the ship. People in Nantucket invest their money in whaling vessels the same way that you invest yours in approved state stocks that bring in good interest.

items.new: So there are cases among them of men who were given Scripture names — a remarkably common fashion on the island — and who in childhood naturally absorbed the stately, dramatic "thee" and "thou" of the Quaker idiom; yet, from the audacious, daring, and boundless adventure of their later lives, they strangely blend with these peculiarities they never outgrew a thousand bold dashes of character not unworthy of a Scandinavian sea-king or a poetical pagan Roman. And when these things unite in a man of greatly superior natural force, with a globular brain and a ponderous heart; who has also, through the stillness and seclusion of many long night watches in the remotest waters, beneath constellations never seen here in the north, been led to think untraditionally and independently; receiving all nature's sweet or savage impressions fresh from her own virgin, voluntary, and confiding breast, and thereby chiefly, though with some help from accidental advantages, learning a bold, sinewy, lofty language — that man makes one in a whole nation's census: a mighty pageant creature, formed for noble tragedies. Nor will it detract from him at all, seen dramatically, if either by birth or by other circumstances he has what seems a half-willful, overruling morbidness at the bottom of his nature. For all men who are tragically great are made so through a certain morbidness. Be sure of this, O young ambition: all mortal greatness is only disease. But we are not yet dealing with such a man — rather with quite another; and still a man whose peculiarity, if he is indeed peculiar, again results only from another phase of the Quaker, modified by individual circumstances.

items.new: Like Captain Peleg, Captain Bildad was a well-to-do, retired whaleman. But unlike Captain Peleg — who didn't care a straw for what are called serious things, and in fact considered those very same serious things the most trifling of all trifles — Captain Bildad had not only been raised from the first in the strictest sect of Nantucket Quakerism, but all his later life at sea, and the sight of many unclothed, lovely island creatures round the Horn — all that had not moved this native-born Quaker one single jot, had not so much as altered one angle of his vest. Still, for all this unchangeableness, there was some lack of plain consistency about worthy Captain Bildad. Though he refused, from conscientious scruples, to bear arms against invaders on land, he had himself boundlessly invaded the Atlantic and the Pacific; and though a sworn enemy of human bloodshed, he had, in his straight-bodied coat, spilled tuns upon tuns of leviathan gore. How the pious Bildad, now in the contemplative evening of his days, reconciled these things in memory, I don't know. But it didn't seem to concern him much, and very probably he had long since come to the wise and sensible conclusion that a man's religion is one thing and this practical world quite another. This world pays dividends. Rising from a little cabin boy in short clothes of the drabbest drab to a harpooner in a broad shad-bellied waistcoat; from that to boat-header, chief mate, and captain, and finally ship owner — Bildad, as I hinted before, had concluded his adventurous career by retiring wholly from active life at the goodly age of sixty and devoting his remaining days to the quiet receiving of his well-earned income.

items.new: I thought him the strangest old Quaker I'd ever seen, especially since Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed like such a blowhard. But I said nothing, only looking around me sharply. Peleg threw open a chest, pulled out the ship's articles, set pen and ink before him, and sat down at a small table. I began to think it was time to figure out what terms I'd accept for the voyage. I already knew that in the whaling business they paid no wages. Instead, everyone, including the captain, received shares of the profits called lays. These lays were proportional to the importance of each man's duties. I also knew that as a green hand at whaling, my own lay wouldn't be large. But considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship, splice a rope, and all that, I had no doubt, from everything I had heard, that I would be offered at least the 275th lay — that is, the 275th part of the clear net proceeds of the voyage, whatever that might amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they called a rather long lay, it was better than nothing. If we had a lucky voyage, it might nearly cover the cost of the clothes I'd wear out, to say nothing of three years' food and board, for which I wouldn't have to pay a penny.

items.new: Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal and responsible owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to impenitent Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he still twitched a little with nervous agitation. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."

items.new: "Come here — closer, closer," said Peleg, with a look in his eye that nearly startled me. "Listen, lad. Never say that aboard the Pequod. Never say it anywhere. Captain Ahab did not name himself. It was a foolish, ignorant whim of his crazy, widowed mother, who died when he was only a year old. And yet the old squaw Tistig, at Gayhead, said the name would somehow prove prophetic. And perhaps other fools like her may tell you the same. I want to warn you — it's a lie. I know Captain Ahab well. I've sailed with him as mate, years ago. I know what he is — a good man. Not a pious, good man like Bildad, but a swearing good man — something like me — only there's a good deal more of him. I'll admit he was never very cheerful. And I know that on the way home last voyage, he was a little out of his mind for a while. But that was the sharp, shooting pains in his bleeding stump — anyone could see that. I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg on the last voyage to that accursed whale, he's been moody — desperately moody, and savage sometimes. But that will pass. And once and for all, let me tell you and assure you, young man: it's better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one. So goodbye — and don't wrong Captain Ahab just because he happens to have a wicked name. Besides, my boy, he has a wife — married not three voyages ago — a sweet, resigned girl. Think about that. By that sweet girl, the old man has a child. Can you hold, then, that there's any utter, hopeless harm in Ahab? No, no, my lad. Stricken and blasted as he may be, Ahab has his humanities!"

items.new: As I walked away, I was full of thoughtfulness. What had been incidentally revealed to me about Captain Ahab filled me with a certain wild, vague painfulness concerning him. And somehow, at the time, I felt a sympathy and a sorrow for him, though for what I don't know, unless it was the cruel loss of his leg. And yet I also felt a strange awe of him; but that sort of awe, which I can't describe at all, was not exactly awe. I don't know what it was. But I felt it, and it didn't turn me against him, though I felt impatient at what seemed like mystery in him, known to me as imperfectly as he was then. Eventually, though, my thoughts were carried off in other directions, so that for the present dark Ahab slipped my mind.

items.new: Toward evening, when I felt sure all his rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked on the door. No answer. I tried to open it, but it was locked from inside. "Queequeg," I said softly through the keyhole. All silent. "I say, Queequeg! Why don't you answer? It's me — Ishmael." But everything stayed still as before. I started to worry. I had given him plenty of time. I thought he might have had a stroke. I looked through the keyhole, but since the door opened into an odd corner of the room, the keyhole view was only a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the footboard of the bed and a strip of wall, nothing more. I was surprised to see the wooden shaft of Queequeg's harpoon leaning against the wall — the landlady had taken it from him the previous evening, before we went up to the room. That's strange, I thought. But since the harpoon was there, and he hardly ever went anywhere without it, he must be inside. No question about it.

items.new: And that's exactly what I did with Queequeg. "Queequeg," I said, "get into bed and lie down and listen to me." I then launched into a review, beginning with the rise and development of primitive religions and working my way down to the various religions of today. Throughout, I tried to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and long hours of squatting in cold, cheerless rooms were complete nonsense — bad for the health, useless for the soul, and contrary to the basic laws of hygiene and common sense. I told him that since he was in other respects such an extremely sensible and shrewd savage, it pained me — deeply pained me — to see him being so foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, I argued, fasting weakens the body, which weakens the spirit, and all thoughts born of fasting are necessarily half-starved. This is the reason why most dyspeptic religious people — those with chronic indigestion — cherish such gloomy notions about their hereafters. In a word, Queequeg, I said, getting somewhat off track: hell is an idea first born from an undigested apple dumpling, and has been perpetuated ever since through the hereditary indigestion caused by Ramadans.

items.new: In the end, I don't think my remarks about religion made much of an impression on Queequeg. In the first place, he seemed somewhat deaf to that particular subject, unless it was approached from his own point of view. In the second place, he didn't understand more than a third of what I said, no matter how simply I put it. And finally, he no doubt believed he knew a good deal more about true religion than I did. items.new: Elijah! I thought. And we walked away, both commenting, each in his own fashion, on this ragged old sailor, and agreed that he was nothing but a humbug trying to be a bugbear. But we had not gone perhaps more than a hundred yards when, happening to turn a corner and looking back as I did so, who should I see but Elijah following us, though at a distance. Somehow the sight of him struck me so that I said nothing to Queequeg about his being behind us, but walked on with my companion, anxious to see whether the stranger would turn the same corner we did. He did; and then it seemed to me that he was dogging us, but with what purpose I could not for the life of me imagine. This, together with his ambiguous, half-hinting, half-revealing, shrouded sort of talk, now bred in me all kinds of vague wonderings and half-fears, all connected with the Pequod; and Captain Ahab; and the leg he had lost; and the Cape Horn fit; and the silver calabash; and what Captain Peleg had said of him when I left the ship the day before; and the prediction of the squaw Tistig; and the voyage we had bound ourselves to sail; and a hundred other shadowy things.

items.new: Everyone knows what a multitude of things — beds, saucepans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nutcrackers, and whatnot — are indispensable for running a household. It's just the same with whaling, which requires three years of housekeeping on the open ocean, far from all grocers, costermongers (street sellers of fruit and vegetables), doctors, bakers, and bankers. This is true of merchant ships too, but nowhere near to the same extent as with whalers. Besides the great length of the voyage and the many specialized items needed for the whale hunt, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors these ships usually visit, you have to remember that of all ships, whalers are the most exposed to accidents of every kind — especially the destruction and loss of the very equipment on which the voyage's success depends. Hence the spare boats, spare spars, spare lines and harpoons, and spare almost everything — everything but a spare captain and a duplicate ship.

items.new: Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once she was properly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for the small of someone's rheumatic back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a sister of charity, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

items.new: During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the ship, and each time I asked about Captain Ahab — how he was and when he planned to come aboard. They always answered that he was getting better and better and was expected any day. In the meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could handle everything needed to ready the vessel. If I had been truly honest with myself, I would have seen plainly that I only half liked the idea of being committed to such a long voyage without once laying eyes on the man who would be its absolute dictator the moment the ship reached open sea. But when a man suspects something is wrong, it sometimes happens that, if he is already caught up in the matter, he unconsciously tries to cover up his suspicions even from himself. And that's exactly what I did. I said nothing and tried to think nothing.

items.new: Now, when getting underway, the pilot usually stations himself at the front of the ship. And there was Bildad, who — along with Peleg, you should know — was one of the port's licensed pilots in addition to his other roles. He was suspected of having got himself licensed just to save the Nantucket pilot fee for every ship he had a stake in, since he never piloted any other vessel. Bildad, I say, could now be seen looking over the bow for the approaching anchor, and at intervals singing what seemed a dismal verse of a psalm to cheer the men at the windlass. They roared out some sort of chorus about the girls in Booble Alley, with hearty good will. This despite the fact that not three days before, Bildad had declared that no profane songs would be permitted aboard the Pequod, especially while getting underway. And Charity, his sister, had placed a small, choice copy of Watts, the hymn-writer, in each seaman's berth.

I was comforting myself with the thought that pious Bildad might offer some salvation, despite his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, when I felt a sudden sharp jab in my rear. Turning around, I was horrified to see Captain Peleg pulling his boot back from my immediate area. That was my first kick.

items.new: It was curious, and not unpleasing, how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this point, especially Captain Bildad. For he was loath to depart, yet; very loath to leave for good a ship bound on so long and perilous a voyage — beyond both stormy Capes; a ship in which some thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested; a ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain, a man almost as old as himself, setting out once more to meet all the terrors of the pitiless jaw; loath to say goodbye to a thing so brimful in every way of every interest to him — poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck with anxious strides; ran down into the cabin to speak another farewell word there; came on deck again and looked to windward; looked toward the wide and endless waters, bounded only by the far-off, unseen Eastern Continents; looked toward the land; looked aloft; looked right and left; looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand and, holding up a lantern, stood for a moment gazing heroically into his face, as much as to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can stand it; yes, I can."

"I hope you'll have fine weather now, so that Captain Ahab may soon be moving among you — a pleasant sun is all he needs, and you'll have plenty of them on the tropic voyage you're going. Be careful in the hunt, you mates. Don't stave the boats needlessly, you harpooners; good white cedar plank has gone up a full three percent within the year. Don't forget your prayers, either. Mr. Starbuck, mind that cooper doesn't waste the spare staves. Oh! The sail needles are in the green locker! Don't whale it too much on the Lord's days, men; but don't miss a fair chance either — that's rejecting Heaven's good gifts. Don't keep that cheese too long down in the hold, Mr. Starbuck; it'll spoil. Be careful with the butter — twenty cents a pound it was, and mind you, if —"
